title: BRICS Culture Ministers’ meet adopts Bhopal Declaration to boost cultural cooperation; focuses on creators’ networking
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The BRICS Culture Ministers’ meet on Saturday (August 8, 2026) adopted the ‘Bhopal Declaration’ aimed at strengthening the institutional framework for cultural cooperation among the member and partner nations, Union Minister for Culture and Tourism Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said.

Addressing media persons in Bhopal, Mr. Shekhawat said that the declaration also provides for enhanced cooperation on provenance research and the return and restitution of cultural property, including exploration of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled tracing tools.

“A key outcome was the adoption of the Bhopal Declaration. Its main aim is to strengthen the institutional framework for BRICS cultural cooperation and provide a shared roadmap covering a wide range of contemporary and traditional areas of culture and heritage,” Mr. Shekhawat said, after the meeting under India’s presidency. 

“A major area of focus of the declaration is cooperation in cultural and creative industries and creative economy which encompasses exchange of methodologies, experiences and best practices, how we can learn from one another, how we can help the creators and artists in, networking and expanding opportunities for them to access markets through digital tools,” he added.

Mr. Shekhawat also said that the declaration also talks about transparency, and fair and equitable remuneration regarding the use of copyright-protected works in AI systems.

The Union Minister also said that the declaration also included provisions to enhance cooperation on UNESCO’s multinational nomination processes, aimed at strengthening a collaborative approach toward the recognition and preservation of shared and interconnected cultural heritage.

“A nation has the chance to nominate one heritage site once in a year but if multiple nations nominate a monument for inscription, whether unilateral, bilateral or multilateral, then there is limit on number,” he said. 

The ministerial meeting was held after three meetings of the Culture Working Group. 

“The BRICS Culture Track under India’s Chairship progressed through three Culture Working Group meetings. The first meeting was held virtually on 29–30 April 2026, followed by the second meeting in Varanasi on 4–5 June 2026 and the third meeting in Bhopal on 5–6 August 2026. The Ministerial Meeting held today [Saturday] witnessed participation from 14 countries, including India, comprising 10 BRICS member countries and four partner countries,” a statement from the Union Ministry of Culture said. 

The Ministry said that the declaration also focuses on safeguarding Traditional Knowledge Systems and Traditional Cultural Expressions; cooperation among museums, libraries and archives in documentary heritage, digitisation and conservation; and protection of creators’ rights.

“As a concrete initiative under the Culture Track, India announced a pilot initiative to develop a Voluntary Artist Registry. The initiative is envisaged to facilitate cultural exchanges, strengthen professional networks and create greater opportunities for artists and creative practitioners across BRICS,” it added.

Earlier on August 6 and 7, a two-day BRICS culture festival was also held in Bhopal.

title: U.S. Vice-President Vance dials PM Modi
author: PTI
content_html:
U.S. Vice-President J.D. Vance dialled Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday (August 8, 2026) to discuss expanding the India-U.S. comprehensive global strategic ties in trade, defence and energy security amid rising tensions in West Asia.

The two leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in emerging technologies and critical minerals.

Mr. Vance’s call to the Prime Minister came days after Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact that was widely seen as a reflection of a new regional alignment amid the West Asia conflict.

During the conversation, PM Modi extended his congratulations to Mr. Vance and Second Lady Usha on the birth of their son.

“Received a phone call from US Vice President JD Vance. We discussed ways to further deepen India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership across key areas,” Mr. Modi said on social media.

“Warmly congratulated him and the Second Lady on the birth of their son and conveyed best wishes to the entire family,” he said.

An Indian readout said Mr. Modi and Mr. Vance reviewed progress in the India-U.S. comprehensive global strategic partnership. “They noted the sustained momentum in the high-level engagements and reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening cooperation in trade, defence, critical and emerging technologies, energy security and critical minerals,” it said. “They also exchanged views on regional and global developments of mutual interest,” it added.

The American side has not yet provided any details of the conversation.

It is not immediately known whether the proposed trade deal between India and the U.S. figured in the talks.

PM Modi and U.S. President Donald Trump, during their meeting in France in June, instructed their officials to work towards a balanced, mutually beneficial and commercially meaningful trade agreement at the earliest.

The relations witnessed a major downturn after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India last year and Mr. Trump made assertions regarding his role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military clashes of May 2025 that drew sharp reaction from Indian officials.

Over the next few months, the U.S. president repeatedly and publicly claimed that he had resolved the military conflict between the two neighbours and saved millions of lives as it was heading toward a full-scale war.

New Delhi stoutly maintained that the cessation of the hostilities was a result of talks between India and Pakistan and the U.S. had nothing to do with it.

Washington’s new immigration policy and its decision to increase the H1B visa fee also contributed to the slide in India-U.S. ties. However, both sides made efforts in the last few months to repair the ties and even moved forward to firm up the trade deal soon.

title: Vidarbha’s farm widows who refuse to remarry
author: Radheshyam  Jadhav
content_html:
In Maharashtra’s drought-prone regions, widow remarriage is gradually shifting from a social taboo to wider acceptance. The shift is partly shaped by the growing number of unmarried farmers struggling to find women willing to marry them. Faced with low incomes, agrarian uncertainty and the social challenges of farming, many such men are now turning to widows. But Radheshyam Jadhav finds that many women are declining these proposals, choosing financial independence and personal autonomy over the complexities that often accompany remarriage

Severe cramps gripped her abdomen. Neelima Renge ached to scream her heart out in anguish and anger. She was eight months pregnant when her husband Moreshwar died by suicide. Crushed under the burden of debt, he decided to end his life. In that haze of grief, anger and pain, she decided never to remarry. More than a decade later, she has not wavered from that decision.

“That decision was correct,” she asserts, standing in the corner of her dingy two-room mud house in Zadgaon, a remote village in Yavatmal district of Vidarbha region, the epicentre of Maharashtra’s farmer suicide crisis.

Inside, a broken charpai (cot), farming tools and stacked soybean sacks leave barely enough room for two people to sit. “This is what I have built on my own — my house and my life,” she says.

Married in 2011, Neelima was unable to complete her secondary school education. Her husband, who cultivated the family’s land, struggled with alcoholism. She says she made every effort to persuade him to stop drinking, but failed. Barely three years into their marriage, he died by suicide, leaving her widowed at the age of 26. A month after his death, she gave birth to a son.

In the years that followed, marriage proposals came through her parents and relatives, while several suitors expressed interest in marrying her, both directly and indirectly.

According to Kishor Tiwari, leader of the farmers’ advocacy and social action group Vidarbha Jan Andolan Samiti, western Vidarbha recorded 30,969 farmer suicides between 2001 and 2024 across Akola, Amravati, Buldhana, Washim and Yavatmal districts. Agrarian distress remains acute, with Yavatmal alone recording 102 farmer suicides between January and May 2026, according to Kishor.

When young women are widowed, their parents often urge them to remarry for financial security and social acceptance.

At times, social activists act as matchmakers, helping widows and prospective grooms connect. In Buldhana, a young farm widow and an unmarried farmer fell in love but, unable to openly announce their intention to marry, sought the help of a local non-profit organisation.

Yet, for widows such as Neelima, whether a man has been married before matters far less than whether he treats her as an equal partner. She did not believe she would find such a relationship and has therefore remained single.

Alongside women widowed by farmer suicides, rural Maharashtra is also home to many never-married farmers who struggle to find wives because of unstable incomes. A network of matchmakers assists these farmers, often searching for prospective brides in the relatively underdeveloped regions of Vidarbha and Marathwada. While prospective grooms initially hesitate to consider widows, many eventually do after repeated rejections from previously unmarried women and their families.

Many widows also turn down proposals from farmers, most of them over the age of 40. They are unwilling to give up their autonomy or risk reliving the trauma of an earlier marriage.

Over the past seven to eight years, the problem has grown into a social crisis. It gained political visibility during the 2024 Lok Sabha election, with both farmers and political parties calling for government intervention.

Navigating life

Neelima’s in-laws declared that she was no longer part of the family and had no claim to its land. They were also resentful that the government compensation released after her husband’s death had been deposited directly into her account rather than theirs.

Neelima took shelter at her parents’ home in Hinganghat, about 55 km from her marital village. She began working as a tailor. Her parents urged her to remarry, arguing that it would be difficult for a young woman to raise a child alone without a man’s support. But even as marriage proposals came her way, Neelima remained convinced that she did not want to step into that “trap” again.

“At the same time, I was terrified about how I would navigate my life and what the future held for my son. I didn’t want to become a burden on my parents and brother. It took me three years to gather the courage to return, knock on my in-laws’ door and demand my share of the land. It was the only source of livelihood for me and my son,” she says.

When her in-laws once again refused to accept her and her son, she insisted on claiming her husband’s share of the land and demanded a meeting of village elders to “do justice”.

Eventually, her in-laws agreed to let her cultivate a three-acre plot. However, they made it clear that its legal ownership would pass only to her son once he attained adulthood. Her in-laws and fellow villagers feared that if Neelima remarried, the land would eventually go to her new husband.

“I was not bothered about what they thought. My priority was to secure a foothold on the land and begin cultivation,” she says, adding that she has successfully experimented with different crops even though her land is entirely rain-fed, with no irrigation facilities. Even now, her relatives and neighbours remain unconvinced that a single woman can survive independently without a man’s support.

Breaking the taboo

Just 22 km from Zadgaon, Chhabutai Waghade, Kusum Aaglane and other women farmers gather at Vanita Shende’s home in Tirzada village. All of them lost their husbands to suicide and have walked a path similar to Neelima’s. They are waiting for the remaining members of their self-help group to arrive. Together, they plan to discuss loan schemes that could support them.

“Life must revolve around men; otherwise, it has no value. That’s what I was taught, and I experience it every day,” says Chhabutai.

Her husband died by suicide after repeated crop failures and mounting debt. Her two daughters are now married. Her brother-in-law seized her land, arguing that a woman without a son “had no need for it”. Living with her widowed mother and having no brothers, Chhabutai says she has spent the past 15 years being reminded that she needs a man’s support. “Yet I have managed well and fought back in my own way,” she says. The other women in the group agree that remarriage often brings more complications than relief.

“Women like us have suffered in marriage, carrying heavy emotional and financial burdens. The thought of remarriage raises one overriding fear: what if the second husband is like the first? That is simply moving from one trauma to another,” says Vanita. Many young widows, she says, were married as children and denied even a basic education. Becoming mothers at a young age and then widows, Vanita adds bitterly, “There was no room for dreams. Here, girls are raised only to marry and bear children.” Kusum and Chhabutai silently affirm her words with a nod.

Women are expected to bear sons, and those who do not are often pressured into repeated pregnancies until they do. Tears well up in Vanita’s eyes and her voice trembles with suppressed anger. Within moments, she regains her composure and says she wants to show what she has achieved on the farmland she wrested from her brother-in-law after a long legal and social struggle.

Walking through her fields, she explains that she adopted farming practices her husband would never have permitted. She has introduced a multi-cropping system and grows vegetables organically. “Men chase only cash crops. If that crop fails, everything is lost,” she says. Stopping at one corner of the field, Vanita points proudly. “This is a turmeric plant.”

Her smile comes after years of struggle. A few years ago, Vanita and a group of farm widows began cultivating turmeric, sending shockwaves through the community. “The turmeric plant is accorded an upper-caste status, and menstruating women are forbidden from cultivating or even approaching it,” she says wryly.

A long-held superstition maintained that the touch, or even the shadow, of a menstruating woman would pollute the crop. Widows were already excluded from haldi-kumkum ceremonies, in which married women exchange turmeric and vermilion as symbols of marital bliss, making it unthinkable for a menstruating widow to handle the plant. Caste and gender taboos intersect closely in local agricultural practices. Yet as families sought alternative sources of livelihood during the COVID-19 pandemic, Vanita broke the taboo. Along with other widows, she planted turmeric in backyards, kitchen gardens, pots and grow bags, tending to the plants through every season and every menstrual cycle.

Today, many women in the region cultivate turmeric in their fields. The belief that men are farmers while women are merely helpers is another stereotype that has been sustained for generations, says Vanita. She adds that she and other farm widows have shown that women can farm successfully without men’s support.

Vanita had, in any case, been fending for herself even while her husband was alive. He had thrown her out after she developed leukoderma, a non-contagious skin condition that causes white patches on the skin. By the time he died by suicide, she had already learned to live independently. Remarriage was never an option. “Even when a man is willing to marry a widow with children, he still expects her to be physically ‘whole’,” she says.

The men and markets

In Buldhana district, social activist D.S. Lahane runs the Manas Foundation, which supports widows and single women seeking remarriage. Working in a region marked by severe agrarian distress, he has observed that many women who approach the foundation eventually decide against remarriage.

Among those open to a second marriage, almost none are willing to marry a farmer, even if it would be the man’s first marriage. Lahane says this reflects a deepening crisis across agrarian Maharashtra. “Despite owning land and earning a modest income, farmers are no longer considered desirable marriage prospects because of the declining social status of farming and the uncertainty of agricultural incomes,” he says.

Many young farmers, he adds, have registered with the foundation in search of brides. Most initially seek previously unmarried women but, after repeated rejections, become willing to marry widows with children.

However, such marriages often bring their own complexities. Women in the region say those who remarry frequently face intense social and familial pressure to have children in their second marriage, even when they do not wish to. Although a previously unmarried man may marry a widow with children, many still want biological children of their own.

In Chikhali, about 40 km from Buldhana, a farm widow with two children received a marriage proposal from a young man from her village whom she already knew. After they married, he insisted on having a child of his own.

“When I gave birth to a son, both my older children began to experience neglect. My elder son, who was old enough to understand what was happening, eventually left to live with my parents. It is deeply painful for me,” she says, requesting anonymity. “Life has become immensely complicated as I try to navigate the demands of being a wife again. Sometimes I think I should have remained unmarried, but I lacked the courage to live entirely on my own in a society that is always ready to exploit a single woman.”

Neelima says choosing to remain single comes at a price. “You can live alone only if you have courage. It requires tremendous resilience and a strong support system of family and friends. Otherwise, women should remarry,” she says.

By choosing to remain single, Neelima, Vanita, Kusum, Chhabutai and many others have challenged deeply entrenched social norms. They continue to wear kumkum and the mangalsutra, traditional symbols of a married Hindu woman. Relatives and fellow villagers routinely criticise them for doing so, objecting to what they see as a violation of local custom.

“We don’t wear them out of attachment. We wear them as protection against predatory behaviour when we travel outside the village. Men often assume that a single or widowed woman is vulnerable and therefore available. To avoid unwanted attention, we wear the mangalsutra and kumkum, even if reluctantly. People in our villages know our circumstances, but this helps protect us when we travel to nearby markets or government offices,” Neelima explains.

When Neelima and Vanita took their soybean and cotton harvest to the Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) at Ralegaon for the first time, they found little encouragement from traders.

“They asked why I had come to the market myself instead of sending the produce through a middleman. I told them I wanted to know the market price of my soybean directly and decide for myself whether to sell it,” Neelima says.

She adds that the sight of women—whether married, widowed or single—selling their produce directly at APMC markets remains unfamiliar and, for many traders and market officials, uncomfortable.

Standing with courage

Yavatmal-based activist Madhuri Khadse, who works with Prerna Gram Vikas Sanstha to help farm widows rebuild their lives, says many widows approach her seeking help to find a husband.

“I ask them why they want to remarry, and the primary reason they give is protection from persistent harassment and unwanted advances,” she says. Young widows, she adds, remain highly vulnerable to exploitation wherever they go, and remarriage is often seen as a means of protection. Simply being perceived as a married woman shields them from much of the abuse they would otherwise face.

Madhuri says that while widow remarriage was traditionally discouraged among some upper-caste farming communities, attitudes have gradually begun to change and marriage proposals are becoming more common.

In a region where thousands of widows are struggling to rebuild their lives, many also face sexual abuse within their own families, a reality documented in several studies, including a 2018 report by the Maharashtra State Commission for Women and Mahila Kisan Adhikar Manch, a nationwide alliance of women farmers. While such abuse is often concealed in villages, everyday actions—such as riding pillion with a man, working alongside male labourers or even speaking to male relatives—are enough to trigger gossip.

Markets, village panchayats, government offices and police stations are rarely welcoming spaces for women. Widows who have built resilient and independent lives must summon additional strength simply to navigate everyday life.

“Even mata (mother) lived this way,” says one woman.

The mata they refer to is Sita. Unlike in many other parts of the country, where idols of Ram, Sita, Laxman and Hanuman are worshipped together, the ancient Sita Mata temple at Raveri in Yavatmal district houses only an idol of Sita. She stands alone in the temple and is especially revered by women. Local belief holds that after being abandoned by Ram, Sita found refuge at Sage Valmiki’s ashram in this region. Stripped of her royal status and forced to endure hardship, she rebuilt her life on her own terms and is believed to have spent the rest of her life here.

Sita’s story later became a powerful symbol of the women’s farmers’ movement in Vidarbha. When the late Sharad Joshi, founder of the Shetkari Sanghatana, helped rebuild the temple, he placed Sita’s legacy at the centre of the 2001 women farmers’ convention held at Raveri. He also developed the concept of “Sita Sheti” (Sita farming), which placed women farmers at the forefront of agricultural decision-making, crop experimentation and household food security.

While much of the country celebrates Ram Navami, many women in this region reserve their celebrations for Sita Navami.

Her brother-in-law seized her land, arguing that a woman without a son “had no need for it”. Living with her widowed mother and having no brothers, Chhabutai says she has spent the past 15 years being reminded that she needs a man’s support. “Yet I have managed well and fought back in my own way,” she says. The other women in the group agree that remarriage often brings more complications than relief.
“Women like us have suffered in marriage, carrying heavy emotional and financial burdens. The thought of remarriage raises one overriding fear: what if the second husband is like the first? That is simply moving from one trauma to another,” says Vanita. Many young widows, she says, were married as children and denied even a basic education. Becoming mothers at a young age and then widows, Vanita adds bitterly, “There was no room for dreams. Here, girls are raised only to marry and bear children.” Kusum and Chhabutai silently affirm her words with a nod.
Women are expected to bear sons, and those who do not are often pressured into repeated pregnancies until they do. Tears well up in Vanita’s eyes and her voice trembles with suppressed anger. Within moments, she regains her composure and says she wants to show what she has achieved on the farmland she wrested from her brother-in-law after a long legal and social struggle.
Walking through her fields, she explains that she adopted farming practices her husband would never have permitted. She has introduced a multi-cropping system and grows vegetables organically. “Men chase only cash crops. If that crop fails, everything is lost,” she says. Stopping at one corner of the field, Vanita points proudly. “This is a turmeric plant.”
Her smile comes after years of struggle. A few years ago, Vanita and a group of farm widows began cultivating turmeric, sending shockwaves through the community. “The turmeric plant is accorded an upper-caste status, and menstruating women are forbidden from cultivating or even approaching it,” she says wryly.
A long-held superstition maintained that the touch, or even the shadow, of a menstruating woman would pollute the crop. Widows were already excluded from
haldi-kumkum
ceremonies, in which married women exchange turmeric and vermilion as symbols of marital bliss, making it unthinkable for a menstruating widow to handle the plant. Caste and gender taboos intersect closely in local agricultural practices. Yet as families sought alternative sources of livelihood during the COVID-19 pandemic, Vanita broke the taboo. Along with other widows, she planted turmeric in backyards, kitchen gardens, pots and grow bags, tending to the plants through every season and every menstrual cycle.
Today, many women in the region cultivate turmeric in their fields. The belief that men are farmers while women are merely helpers is another stereotype that has been sustained for generations, says Vanita. She adds that she and other farm widows have shown that women can farm successfully without men’s support.
Vanita had, in any case, been fending for herself even while her husband was alive. He had thrown her out after she developed leukoderma, a non-contagious skin condition that causes white patches on the skin. By the time he died by suicide, she had already learned to live independently. Remarriage was never an option. “Even when a man is willing to marry a widow with children, he still expects her to be physically ‘whole’,” she says.
The men and markets
In Buldhana district, social activist D.S. Lahane runs the Manas Foundation, which supports widows and single women seeking remarriage. Working in a region marked by severe agrarian distress, he has observed that many women who approach the foundation eventually decide against remarriage.
Among those open to a second marriage, almost none are willing to marry a farmer, even if it would be the man’s first marriage. Lahane says this reflects a deepening crisis across agrarian Maharashtra. “Despite owning land and earning a modest income, farmers are no longer considered desirable marriage prospects because of the declining social status of farming and the uncertainty of agricultural incomes,” he says.
Many young farmers, he adds, have registered with the foundation in search of brides. Most initially seek previously unmarried women but, after repeated rejections, become willing to marry widows with children.
However, such marriages often bring their own complexities. Women in the region say those who remarry frequently face intense social and familial pressure to have children in their second marriage, even when they do not wish to. Although a previously unmarried man may marry a widow with children, many still want biological children of their own.
In Chikhali, about 40 km from Buldhana, a farm widow with two children received a marriage proposal from a young man from her village whom she already knew. After they married, he insisted on having a child of his own.
“When I gave birth to a son, both my older children began to experience neglect. My elder son, who was old enough to understand what was happening, eventually left to live with my parents. It is deeply painful for me,” she says, requesting anonymity. “Life has become immensely complicated as I try to navigate the demands of being a wife again. Sometimes I think I should have remained unmarried, but I lacked the courage to live entirely on my own in a society that is always ready to exploit a single woman.”
Neelima says choosing to remain single comes at a price. “You can live alone only if you have courage. It requires tremendous resilience and a strong support system of family and friends. Otherwise, women should remarry,” she says.
By choosing to remain single, Neelima, Vanita, Kusum, Chhabutai and many others have challenged deeply entrenched social norms. They continue to wear
kumkum
and the
mangalsutra
, traditional symbols of a married Hindu woman. Relatives and fellow villagers routinely criticise them for doing so, objecting to what they see as a violation of local custom.
“We don’t wear them out of attachment. We wear them as protection against predatory behaviour when we travel outside the village. Men often assume that a single or widowed woman is vulnerable and therefore available. To avoid unwanted attention, we wear the
mangalsutra
and
kumkum
, even if reluctantly. People in our villages know our circumstances, but this helps protect us when we travel to nearby markets or government offices,” Neelima explains.
When Neelima and Vanita took their soybean and cotton harvest to the Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) at Ralegaon for the first time, they found little encouragement from traders.
“They asked why I had come to the market myself instead of sending the produce through a middleman. I told them I wanted to know the market price of my soybean directly and decide for myself whether to sell it,” Neelima says.
She adds that the sight of women—whether married, widowed or single—selling their produce directly at APMC markets remains unfamiliar and, for many traders and market officials, uncomfortable.
Standing with courage
Yavatmal-based activist Madhuri Khadse, who works with Prerna Gram Vikas Sanstha to help farm widows rebuild their lives, says many widows approach her seeking help to find a husband.
“I ask them why they want to remarry, and the primary reason they give is protection from persistent harassment and unwanted advances,” she says. Young widows, she adds, remain highly vulnerable to exploitation wherever they go, and remarriage is often seen as a means of protection. Simply being perceived as a married woman shields them from much of the abuse they would otherwise face.
Madhuri says that while widow remarriage was traditionally discouraged among some upper-caste farming communities, attitudes have gradually begun to change and marriage proposals are becoming more common.
In a region where thousands of widows are struggling to rebuild their lives, many also face sexual abuse within their own families, a reality documented in several studies, including a 2018 report by the Maharashtra State Commission for Women and Mahila Kisan Adhikar Manch, a nationwide alliance of women farmers. While such abuse is often concealed in villages, everyday actions—such as riding pillion with a man, working alongside male labourers or even speaking to male relatives—are enough to trigger gossip.
Markets, village panchayats, government offices and police stations are rarely welcoming spaces for women. Widows who have built resilient and independent lives must summon additional strength simply to navigate everyday life.
“Even
mata
(mother) lived this way,” says one woman.
The
mata
they refer to is Sita. Unlike in many other parts of the country, where idols of Ram, Sita, Laxman and Hanuman are worshipped together, the ancient Sita Mata temple at Raveri in Yavatmal district houses only an idol of Sita. She stands alone in the temple and is especially revered by women. Local belief holds that after being abandoned by Ram, Sita found refuge at Sage Valmiki’s ashram in this region. Stripped of her royal status and forced to endure hardship, she rebuilt her life on her own terms and is believed to have spent the rest of her life here.
Sita’s story later became a powerful symbol of the women’s farmers’ movement in Vidarbha. When the late Sharad Joshi, founder of the Shetkari Sanghatana, helped rebuild the temple, he placed Sita’s legacy at the centre of the 2001 women farmers’ convention held at Raveri. He also developed the concept of “Sita
Sheti
” (Sita farming), which placed women farmers at the forefront of agricultural decision-making, crop experimentation and household food security.
While much of the country celebrates Ram Navami, many women in this region reserve their celebrations for Sita Navami.

title: Tech-savvy Anubhava Mantapa expected to open in May, 2027, in Basavakalyan
author: Nagesh Prabhu
content_html:
The colossal Anubhava Mantapa — under construction at Basavakalyan in Bidar district and conceived as a tribute to the eponymous 12th-century concept of philosopher, poet, and religious leader Basaveshwara — seeks to recreate the spirit of what is widely regarded as the world’s earliest “spiritual and socio-philosophical Parliament”.

The edifice is envisioned as a centre for preserving and promoting the egalitarian ideals, reformist philosophy, and the literary legacy of the Sharanas, or followers of Basaveshwara, in the Veerashaiva-Lingayat tradition.

The Mantapa, conceived in 2017 and under construction since June 2022, is expected to be inaugurated in May 2027. Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar recently reviewed the progress of the project, said P.K. Sharma, Project Manager of B.G. Shirke Construction Technology Pvt. Ltd. It will be named ‘Anubhava Mantapa — Monument of Democracy’.

The monument is expected to reinforce Basavakalyan as the cradle of the 12th-century Sharana movement of Karnataka. | Photo Credit: K. BHAGYA PRAKASH

Scholarship and tourism

Together with the nearby 108-foot Basaveshwara statue, the historic Akkanagamma Cave and the Allama Prabhu Math, the monument is expected to establish Basavakalyan as a major destination for pilgrimage, scholarship, and cultural tourism, while reinforcing its place as the cradle of the 12th-century Sharana movement of Karnataka, which played a key role in shaking the caste and gender hierarchies of the time. It also reshaped Kannada literature.

Spread over nearly five acres and being built at a cost of more than ₹800 crore, the six-storeyed Anubhava Mantapa structure is crowned by an 183-ft. Shivalinga-shaped dome. The monument features 770 columns (pillars), each engraved with one of the Vachanas of the 770 Sharanas of the 12th century, symbolising the movement’s enduring literary and spiritual heritage, according to Babasaheb Gadde, chairman of Nurture and Nature Enterprises and the project’s consultant. The names of 12,944 martyrs of India’s freedom struggle have also been inscribed on its walls as a tribute to their sacrifice.

Spread over nearly five acres and being built at a cost of more than ₹800 crore, the six-storeyed Anubhava Mantapa structure is crowned by an 183-ft Shivalinga-shaped dome. | Photo Credit: K. BHAGYA PRAKASH

The six floors of the monument correspond to the six stages of spiritual evolution — Bhaktasthala, Maheshasthala, Prasadisthala, Pranalingisthala, Sharanasthala, and Aikyasthala. | Photo Credit: K. BHAGYA PRAKASH

The structure has been designed around the Ashtavarna principles of Sharana philosophy — Guru, Linga, Jangama, Vibhuti, Rudrakshi, Padodaka, Prasada, and Mantra. The names of 74 democratic countries will be inscribed on monolithic stone pillars outside the monument, with each pillar highlighting the distinctive features and democratic traditions of the respective country.

The monument itself symbolically represents the Sharana philosophy. Its six floors correspond to the six stages of spiritual evolution — Bhaktasthala, Maheshasthala, Prasadisthala, Pranalingisthala, Sharanasthala, and Aikyasthala. The inner circular structure, representing the soul, rises through all six floors and is surrounded by a water body at the ground level. A middle ring, symbolising the body, contains three interconnected floors, while the outer ring will be developed with landscaped gardens and public spaces.

The Anubhava Mantapa under construction at Basavakalyan in Bidar district in Karnataka. | Photo Credit: K. BHAGYA PRAKASH

Digital classrooms

The ground floor will house 16 digital classrooms dedicated to teaching Basavanna’s Kayaka (dignity of labour) philosophy alongside modern skill development programmes, including technology-oriented courses aimed at preparing students and the youth for an AI-driven economy.

The first floor, Bhaktasthala, will feature 12 theatres, each spread over about 3,500 sq. ft., showcasing the philosophy, history, and social reforms of the Sharanas through immersive multimedia presentations.

The second floor will house a Kayaka Museum, where aptitude assessments and interactive exhibits will help students identify their strengths and aptitudes while encouraging skill-based learning.

The third floor will include a Kayaka Village, meditation facilities, and a robotics centre equipped with a 7-D theatre. The meditation centre is intended to demonstrate the transformative effects of meditation and support awareness campaigns against drug abuse, alcoholism, and smoking. Visitors will also be able to interact with AI-enabled systems and seek information on a range of subjects in Kannada and other languages.

The monument is expected to establish Basavakalyan as a major destination for pilgrimage, scholarship and cultural tourism. | Photo Credit: K. BHAGYA PRAKASH

The fourth floor is to be designed as a Parliament hall, where sessions of the Karnataka Legislature could be held on special occasions. It will also house a 400-seat auditorium for lectures, seminars, and public discussions. One of its proposed features is a “truth test” facility intended to encourage ethical reflection among elected representatives and public officials.

A whispering gallery will occupy the fifth floor, while the sixth floor, Aikyasthala, will house what is proposed to be one of the world’s largest Shivalingas, sculpted from nearly 4,000 slabs of black stone.

Blending history, philosophy, spirituality and modern technology, the monument seeks not merely to commemorate Basavanna’s legacy but to create a living institution dedicated to dialogue, ethical governance, knowledge, and social transformation, said Dr. Gadde.

Anubhava Mantapa under construction at Basavakalyan in Bidar district in Karnataka. | Photo Credit: K. BHAGYA PRAKASH

title: Vishnu idol unearthed in Ranipet
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Little did a group of residents who stumbled on a stone idol while walking on the dry Palar riverbed at Puliyankannu village on Saturday know that they had unearthed a 500-year-old treasure - a Lord Vishnu idol.

Residents said that they were returning home from Walajah town to the village when one of the persons stumbled upon the idol, which was buried. They removed a portion of sand around the idol and found a damaged sculpture. “We are surprised to notice the idol as the dry river was our routine route to reach nearby villages and towns,” said R. Mari, a resident.

Residents alerted the village headman, who in turn, informed the police and village administrative officer (VAO). After pain-staking efforts by removing sand from all four sides of the treasure for nearly an hour, workers lifted the stone idol with a mechanised crane in the presence of revenue officials and the police.

Revenue officials said that the head of the Vishnu idol, which is two-feet tall and 1.5-feet wide, was slightly damaged. Two arms, including the one that holds the chakra on the right side of the idol, was intact. Local historians said that the Vishnu idol could be around 500 years old and belong to the Vijayanagara era because it was during this period that the region witnessed more temple-related constructions.

Like Sriperumbudur (the birthplace of saint Ramanuja), the region along Palar River was also a great centre for both Vaishnavites and Shaivites. The Vijayanagara rulers were mostly Vaishnavites, they said.

Revenue officials said that under the Indian Treasure Trove Act 1878, anything found below one feet depth belongs to the government. As per norms, such treasure should be handed over to the district treasury with the Collector being the sole guardian of the treasure. At present, the idol has been kept at the Taluk Office in Walajah town.

Officials of Arcot Site Museum said that a request was to be made to Collector Priya Ravichandran for public display of the granite idol at Arcot Museum as such a measure will help students and other public learn the rich past of the region.

Earlier, such an idol was unearthed from Mellur village near Katpadi in 2008. The five-feet Vishnu idol made of sandstone was the tallest statue, dating to the early Chola period of 9th century at the museum.

title: Litigants affected as advocates stay away from court proceedings in Vellore
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Litigants were badly affected as advocates stayed away from court proceedings at the Combined Court Complex in Vellore since August 5, demanding permanent canteen facilities.

Unaware of the boycott of courts by law practitioners, several litigants visited the court complex in Vellore town. Cases that came up for hearing in these courts were adjourned. “We travel long distances to attend court proceedings. We have skipped work many times to ensure that we are able to come to the court when the cases are listed. Such boycott affects poor litigants,” said V. Ramu, a litigant.

Every day, on an average, more than 3,000 litigants visit the court complex in Vellore. The complex comprises 15 courts that handle civil and criminal cases. Around 600 advocates are working as regular practitioners in each of these courts. On an average, over 300-400 cases come up at courts every day. Currently, 1,500-2,000 cases are pending before each court in these districts.

Court officials said that the District Court had a full-fledged canteen facility for more than two decades before it was closed by the Public Works Department (PWD), which maintains the court, before the COVID-19 pandemic. The PWD had cited that it plans to run the facility with modern facilities. However, the old canteen remained locked.

Court officials said that since then, advocates, court staff, litigants have to walk at least 500 metres to have food at roadside eateries. As court proceedings take longer hours, a refreshment kiosk inside the premises will help litigants and staff to take a small break and attend court proceedings on time. “Going away from court premises for refreshments will delay court proceedings. In fact, cases that are listed for hearing will be adjourned to a later date due to such delays,” said a court official. 

Court officials said that members of the Bar Association gave a petition to M. Elavarasan, Principal District Judge, Vellore, requesting him to take necessary steps to set up a full-fledged canteen in the premises.

title: Tamil Nadu Budget 2026: a taxing task for TVK-led government
author: T. Ramakrishnan
content_html:
S. Mala, 38, a casual labourer who hails from Gingee in Villupuram district, says she had, for nearly 20 years, voted for the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam. But, for this year’s Assembly election, she shifted her allegiance to the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam because of a couple of enticing promises: an increase in the monthly honorarium for women to ₹2,500 and free travel for women in inter-district bus services. “I expected that the TVK-led government would implement at least one or both of them this year,” she says.

R. Selvakumar, an Information Technology professional, who hails from Nachipalayam in Tiruppur district, also made a political shift this election — from the AIADMK to the TVK — in the hope that the fledgling party would qualitatively enhance government intervention in education and health. Mr. Selvakumar has a couple of school-going children, and he had hoped that greater attention would be paid to the improvement of infrastructure, both physical and digital, in schools run by the government. “Yes, the government has made a beginning with the Super Clean Super Campus scheme. I wish it had extended the programme to all the schools.”

Though belonging to diverse backgrounds, Ms. Mala and Mr. Selvakumar are not bowled over by the TVK’s maiden Budget — for different reasons.

Opposite stance

Taking a diametrically opposite stance, industries and chambers of commerce have been describing the Budget as progressive with focus on growth and industrial development.

But the situation seems to be that of “willing to strike, but afraid to wound”. On the one hand, the government is conscious of the need for fiscal consolidation. On the other, it wants to honour its election promises, at least the key ones. Both in the White Paper and in the Budget, the government made the right noises.

In the White Paper, the government said, “Correcting it [fiscal deterioration] will require a sustained and disciplined effort across revenue mobilisation, expenditure management, PSU [public sector undertakings] reform, and debt management — an effort that extends well beyond any single Budget cycle. So, the fiscal space available for taking up new programmes during the year can only be very minimal and cutting down on leakages, restoring best practices to weed out corruption, and finding avenues for additional resource mobilisation without burdening the citizens is the only way forward for a sustainable fiscal management.”

In his inaugural Budget speech on August 5, Finance Minister N. Marie Wilson was quite candid. “The fiscal position of the State is in the red, and we have been handed a treasury box that is overburdened with debt and sub-optimal income with leaking holes. The repair has been started, but we would need at least two years to bring the financial administration back to the track of fiscal prudence.”

At the same time, the government does not want to be seen as wavering on its election assurances. On the day he assumed office, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay cleared the proposal to increase coverage of the free electricity scheme to 200 units from 100 units for those residential connections that consume up to 500 units bimonthly. For the crop loan waiver, his government first said that only small and marginal farmers with loans up to ₹50,000 each would be covered. Later, it expanded the coverage to ₹75,000, regardless of the size of landholding. The government, which is working on giving a one-gram gold ring to children born at government hospitals after September 15, also announced in the Budget its plan to implement another scheme — ‘Annan Seer’ — to give an eight-gram gold coin and a silk sari to every woman beneficiary.

Relief to rural community

K.R. Shanmugam, the government’s economic consultant and former Director of the Madras School of Economics, points out that the government’s decision to distribute free milch cows to the rural poor will provide relief to the community if this year’s Super El Niño has a severe adverse climate impact.

Notwithstanding the government’s optimism, seasoned specialists feel that the government, aware of the precarious financial health of the State, should not have undertaken to implement schemes such as free electricity for additional 100 units and the crop loan waiver, both of which will cost the exchequer nearly ₹7,480 crore.

As regards the crop loan waiver, the government could have loosened its purse only to those who are in distress and who badly require its assistance, after a thorough study. Particularly, farmers in water-deficit southern districts require preferential treatment. The blanket crop loan waiver could have waited as, after all, the Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation, during the ongoing procurement year (2025-26), recorded an all-time high purchase of nearly 63 lakh tonnes from around 6.16 lakh farmers. In addition to the minimum support price (MSP) being provided by the Union government, the State gave around ₹917 crore in incentives to the farmers.

Government employees disappointed

The government employees, who had been expecting the TVK government to restore the Old Pension Scheme (OPS), were disappointed, as the allocation for pension and retirement benefits has been reduced by at least ₹11,000 crore (set apart by the previous DMK government in the interim Budget early this year towards an additional contribution to the Tamil Nadu Assured Pension Scheme). There is no hint in the Budget on what the TVK government intends to do with regard to this pension scheme.

Conscious of its financial condition, Mr. Vijay’s government is taking steps to raise resources additionally to the tune of ₹15,000 crore this year through various measures. It has constituted a committee, headed by veteran economist Montek Singh Ahluwalia, to suggest means of revenue augmentation. At the same time, the government knows well that it does not have much freedom to raise resources at will, after the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime came into force.

Revenue-sharing model

It is in this context that the suggestion made by former Chief Secretary and Finance Secretary of the Tamil Nadu government, K. Shanmugam, in an article published in The Hindu on October 17, 2025, assumes relevance. He suggested that the Centre share with States the personal income tax base on a 50:50 basis. Or, the States can be empowered to top up I-T without major changes to the current system of levy and collection. His point is that this would reduce the States’ fiscal dependence on the Centre, improve liquidity, and allow progressive States — which contribute more tax revenue — to directly benefit from their higher tax base.

The TVK-led government, which relies on the Congress, two Left parties, and the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi for its survival, does not want to adopt a confrontationist approach towards the Bharatiya Janata Party-led government at the Centre. It knows that the Union government’s support will help to ease the tight fiscal position. It has to not only learn the art of tightrope walking more but also to master it.

title: Abhishek Banerjee’s personal assistant grilled for 10 hours by Bengal police
author: Shiv Sahay Singh
content_html:
Two days after the Supreme Court granted the go-ahead to arrest Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee’s personal assistant Sumit Roy, he appeared before the West Bengal Police on Saturday (August 8, 2026) for interrogation.

Mr. Roy had been in hiding after the defeat of Trinamool Congress in the West Bengal Assembly polls. Several cases of fraud, including a land grab case at Salboni, were registered against him. He appeared at Bhabani Bhawan, the West Bengal Police headquarters, at 10 a.m. in the morning and was questioned till late in the evening.

The questioning of Mr. Roy assumes significance as he was closely linked to Trinamool Congress leader Abhishek Banerjee as his personal assistant. There have been 16 FIRs filed against the Trinamool Congress general secretary after the change of regime in West Bengal.

A few weeks ago, a team of police in Salboni had tried to break into a south Kolkata residence of Mr. Banerjee looking for his personal assistant. Other than the Salboni land grab case, there are at least two more cases against Mr. Roy. Earlier this week, Mr. Roy approached the Calcutta High Court seeking urgent hearing of the cases. Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya dismissed the petition for urgent listing and said that the hearing will be held as per the list.

‘Probe will reach Abhishek’

Leader of Opposition in the West Bengal Assembly Ritabrata Banerjee said Mr. Roy is a crucial link to Camac Street (often referred to as the office of Abhishek Banerjee) and soon the investigators will reach Abhishek Banerjee too.

Meanwhile, former Trinamool Congress MLA Sanat Dey was on Saturday arrested in State’s North 24 Parganas district over allegations of extortion and post-poll violence, police said.

Mr. Dey, former MLA of Naihati, was arrested as he is accused of extortion, land grabbing and attacks on BJP workers following the 2021 Assembly elections.

Local residents of Naihati earlier claimed that the former MLA had unleashed a reign of terror across the Naihati region and issued threats prior to election results. Several former MLAs of the Trinamool Congress and councillors were arrested on charges of extortion and electoral violence after the BJP came to power in West Bengal.
